extracted.intended_audience: conference reviewers, area chairs, program chairs, and ML researchers interested in peer review practices
extracted.subtask_description: Reflections on the NIPS 2014 reviewing experiment and practical guidance about how reviewers, area chairs, and program chairs handled paper discussion, decision-making, and quality control during a large conference review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss non-obvious papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewers discussed any paper that wasn’t immediately an obvious, high-confidence consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers that are not clear accepts/rejects should be brought into discussion rather than disposed of by scores alone; discussion is the first step before area chair review and escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area chairs must examine reviews and join discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Area chairs examined all these reviews, papers, discussions, joining in the discussion in most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs are expected to read reviews and participate actively in the reviewer discussions rather than passively relying on reviewer scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on average scores; use richer heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Nowhere in this process does the average score even come up other than as a very rough way for area chairs to sort the papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use better heuristics to sort and prioritize papers for discussion — e.g., controversiality, spread of scores, and low confidence scores — instead of making decisions based solely on mean reviewer scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews must be substantive, supported, timely, and proofread
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reviews reported opinions that were unsubstantiated, unsupported in the review writeups, late, and unproofread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reviews should provide supporting arguments/evidence for their opinions, be submitted on time, and be readable (proofread) so area chairs and other reviewers can act on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers should engage in post-review discussion and rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers with crappy reviews became very hard to reach. They didn’t participate in the discussion without a ton of prodding, they didn’t respond to the author rebuttals, and when they did respond, they surprisingly tended to stick to their original, seemingly unsubstantiated opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are expected to participate in discussion, respond to rebuttals, and be willing to revise or justify their opinions rather than ignoring follow-up or clinging to unsupported initial judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-level adjudication and escalation for borderline papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Area chairs met in pairs to go over all their papers together, making pair judgement calls on each and identifying controversial or tricky decisions that needed to be discussed at the larger meetings. After that, the chairs met in groups of four with one of the program chairs to go over these tricky decisions. ... anytime we couldn’t reach a decision, it was marked for further discussion and consideration as a borderline paper by the next level of the hierarchy: the program chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hierarchical process (AC pairs -> groups with program chairs -> program chairs) to resolve difficult or borderline cases; explicitly mark and escalate papers that cannot be decided at a lower level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area chairs should assess reviewer validity and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: It was clear to me how thoughtfully my partner had considered the reviews and the papers, understanding when reviewers were making valid arguments and when they were being unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs should critically evaluate whether reviewers' arguments are valid or unfair and weigh reviews accordingly — i.e., find signal in the noise rather than treating all reviews as equally informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer confidence must be demonstrated in review text
rubrics_metrics.description: The easy decisions, where all reviewers agreed, reported high confidence, and demonstrated high confidence through their words, were very quick discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric confidence scores are insufficient alone; reviewers who report high confidence should show that confidence through clear, substantive explanations in the review text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area chairs need access to author identities for conflict management
rubrics_metrics.description: Area chairs, who had access to author identities (because we are partially responsible for preventing conflicts of interest), could in fact see if a paper was a duplicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs should have access to author identities at least to the extent required to detect conflicts of interest and duplicates; this role-based access has implications for blinding and experimental setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain experimental blinding and avoid identifiable artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the experiment work on CMT, the program chairs had to create a fake additional author, whose name was something like NIPS Dup1. So it was pretty obvious. ... This fact surely contaminates the experimental results and any conclusions we might be able to definitely make about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing experiments on reviewing systems, avoid introducing obvious or identifiable artifacts (e.g., fake author names) that could alert reviewers/ACs and bias behavior; ensure experimental integrity and proper blinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference peer review should focus on selecting content, not assigning credit
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of these huge processes is not to assign credit for peoples’ work, it’s to decide what content to present in a conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criteria and process design for conferences should prioritize selecting work appropriate for presentation (quality, relevance) rather than treating conference review as the main mechanism for awarding scholarly credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address scaling problems with reviewer training or workload redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: As NIPS continues expanding to accommodate the growing interest in its topics, we’ll have to figure out how to address the growing proportion of bad reviewers that we’ll need to recruit to handle its scale. Maybe the answer is better reviewer training, or maybe the answer is more work for the more competent reviewers, or maybe there is no answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain review quality as conferences grow, consider interventions like improved reviewer training programs, reallocating more work to competent reviewers, or other systemic changes to reduce the impact of low-quality reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use aggregation and higher-level oversight to correct individual misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers almost never understand the papers I submit... For me, the answer is pretty close to always [the final decision is right]. ... Maybe despite reviewers not knowing what they’re reading, their B.S. detectors still work fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that individual reviewers may misunderstand papers; rely on aggregation of reviews, AC judgment, and program-chair oversight to arrive at correct final decisions, rather than expecting every reviewer to fully understand every paper.
